design_detail: Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2016 comparative risk assessment for alcohol by the GBD 2016 Alcohol Collaborators (more than 500 named collaborators; analysis led by the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, Seattle). Exposure (prevalence of current drinking and average grams of ethanol a day among current drinkers) was modelled for 195 locations, 1990–2016, both sexes and 5-year age groups from 15 to 95 and older, from 694 sources (121,029 data points), combining sales data adjusted for tourism and unrecorded alcohol with survey data. Dose–response relative-risk curves for 23 outcomes were fitted to 3,992 relative-risk estimates from 592 cohort and case-control studies found in a new systematic review (details only in appendix 1). A theoretical minimum risk exposure level (TMREL) was taken as the minimum of one weighted average of the 23 curves, each weighted by that outcome's global age-standardised DALY rate in 2016 (both sexes); population attributable fractions from exposure, relative risks and the TMREL were applied to GBD 2016 deaths and DALYs, with alcohol use disorders assigned an attributable fraction of 1. Design 'modelling' as the round brief directs for attributable-burden estimates: no risk-of-bias instrument applies, so the card states the design's limits (METHODS §5.3).
can_establish: Model-based estimates, under GBD 2016's stated inputs and assumptions, of the prevalence of current drinking and average consumption by location, age and sex, of deaths and DALYs attributable to alcohol, of the shape of each cause-specific relative-risk curve as fitted to the observational studies, and of the intake that minimises one globally DALY-weighted average of those curves.
cannot_establish: That any amount of alcohol harms a given person or every population (the zero minimum comes from one globally weighted curve whose interval reaches 0.8 drinks a day and which moved to about half a drink a day when the same group changed the weights in 2022); causal effects beyond what the underlying observational studies can support; the risk of particular drinking patterns (only average volume is modelled); or burden in people under 15 and harm to others beyond road injuries.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (modelling). Exposure sources were found through the Global Health Data Exchange (GHDx) and PubMed; relative-risk studies through PubMed, the GHDx and the reference lists of earlier meta-analyses. The relative-risk studies together covered about 28 million people and 649,000 registered cases of the outcomes (Methods › Data sources, 1st paragraph). Search strategy, flow diagrams, the list of sources and the cause-specific curves are in appendix 1 (pp 52–146), which was not read.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Outcomes were chosen by reviewing prospective and observational studies and judging causality with Bradford Hill's criteria; 23 outcomes were included (Methods › Study design, 2nd paragraph). People younger than 15 were not modelled because data were sparse; outcomes with accumulating but insufficient evidence, such as dementia and psoriasis, were left out (Discussion, 6th paragraph). Eligibility criteria for individual studies, search dates and language limits are not given in the main text.
sample.demographics: Not applicable. Estimates cover 195 locations, both sexes and 5-year age groups from 15 to 95 and older, 1990–2016.
sample.selection_effects: Relative risks come from observational studies whose participants and reference groups differ. Whether former drinkers were counted among abstainers was tested as a study-level covariate and kept only where significant: for ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke and diabetes (Methods › Systematic review and meta-analysis, 2nd paragraph); for the other 20 outcomes no reference-group adjustment is reported. No appraisal of the quality of the 592 studies is described in the main text. Survey exposure data are self-reported and were rescaled to sales data.

exposure.measurement: Modelled. Population alcohol stock (litres per capita) came from sales data, adjusted by adding alcohol drunk abroad by residents and subtracting alcohol drunk by tourists (World Tourism Organization data), and by adding unrecorded alcohol (illicit production, home brewing, local beverages) drawn 1000 times from a uniform distribution between zero and the average of published estimates for each location, which the authors call conservative. Survey estimates of current drinking, abstention and grams a day by age and sex were rescaled to sum to that stock (Methods › Data sources, 2nd to 5th paragraphs).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Exposure is average daily volume: grams of pure ethanol a day among current drinkers, reported in standard drinks of 10 g. Current drinking = at least one drink in the past 12 months; abstention = no alcohol in the past year (Introduction, 7th paragraph; Figure 1 legend). Curves were fitted between 0 and 12.5 standard drinks a day, beyond which there were no data. Drinking pattern (heavy episodic drinking) is not modelled, which the authors list as a limitation (Discussion, 6th paragraph). Survey volumes by beverage were converted to ethanol with assumed average strengths (appendix 1, p 50, not read).
exposure.polysubstance: Not modelled. Tobacco and other drug use enter only through whatever adjustment each underlying study made; joint effects (for example of alcohol and smoking on cancers of the mouth and throat) are not addressed in the main text.

comparison.controls: Two counterfactuals. For the relative risks: the abstaining or non-drinking category of each underlying study, whose make-up varied (adjusted for the inclusion of former drinkers only for ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke and diabetes). For attributable burden: the estimated TMREL of zero standard drinks a day, which the authors present as estimated rather than assumed (Introduction, 6th paragraph; Methods › Systematic review and meta-analysis, 3rd paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable at model level. In the underlying studies, illness that makes people stop drinking (the sick-quitter problem) and survival bias are handled only through the reference-category covariate and the average age of participants (Introduction, 4th paragraph); other ways in which lifelong abstainers differ from people who drink are not addressed in the main text (editors' observation).

outcomes.instruments: GBD 2016 estimates of deaths and DALYs by cause, location, age, sex and year for 23 alcohol-associated outcomes (the list is in appendix 1; the GBD 2020 paper names the same 23: ischaemic stroke, intracerebral haemorrhage, ischaemic heart disease, hypertensive heart disease, atrial fibrillation and flutter, eight cancers, type 2 diabetes, cirrhosis and other chronic liver disease, pancreatitis, idiopathic epilepsy, tuberculosis, lower respiratory infection, transport injuries, unintentional injuries, self-harm and interpersonal violence). Road-injury burden falling on people other than the drinker was redistributed with US Fatality Analysis Reporting System data, assumed to hold everywhere (Methods › Attributable burden due to alcohol use, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: The paper states that it follows the GATHER reporting guideline (Methods › Study design, 1st paragraph). No check of the weighted curve against all-cause mortality is reported.
outcomes.operationalization: Attributable burden = population attributable fraction (from exposure, relative risk and TMREL) × deaths or DALYs for each outcome, summed over outcomes and aggregated by Socio-demographic Index (SDI) quintile. The TMREL is the minimum of a single weighted average of the cause-specific curves, weights being each outcome's global, age-standardised DALY rate per 100,000 in 2016 for both sexes (Methods › Systematic review and meta-analysis, 3rd paragraph). 'Health loss' thus means DALY-weighted risk over 23 outcomes; all-cause mortality was not analysed.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: estimation with uncertainty intervals; 'significant' is used only for curve shapes and for the sensitivity analysis, without stated tests.

analysis.effect_sizes: All intervals are 95% uncertainty intervals; standard drink = 10 g ethanol; current drinking = any drink in the past 12 months. Prevalence of current drinking in 2016: 32.5% (30.0–35.2) of people worldwide, 25% (23–27) of females and 39% (36–43) of males, 2.4 billion people; mean consumption 0.73 (0.68–0.78) standard drinks a day in females and 1.7 (1.5–1.9) in males. Attributable deaths 2.8 million (2.4–3.3); 2.2% (1.5–3.0) of age-standardised female deaths and 6.8% (5.8–8.0) of male deaths; 1.6% (1.4–2.0) of female and 6.0% (5.4–6.7) of male DALYs; seventh leading risk factor. Ages 15–49: leading risk factor; 3.8% (3.2–4.3) of female and 12.2% (10.8–13.6) of male deaths; 2.3% (2.0–2.6) of female and 8.9% (7.8–9.9) of male DALYs. Cause-specific curves (relative to each study's non-drinking category): significant J-shape only for ischaemic heart disease, minimum relative risk 0.86 (0.80–0.96) in men at 0.83 drinks a day and 0.82 (0.72–0.95) in women at 0.92 drinks a day; non-significant dips for diabetes and ischaemic stroke; all other outcomes, including all cancers, rising with intake. TMREL of the weighted curve: zero (0.0–0.8) standard drinks a day.
analysis.covariates: In the relative-risk meta-regressions: a study-level covariate for the composition of the reference category, kept for ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke and diabetes, and the average age of participants (Introduction, 4th paragraph; Methods › Systematic review and meta-analysis, 2nd paragraph). Other covariates, and the model in detail, are only in appendix 1 (pp 51–138).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the paper states adherence to the GATHER statement. Raw data underlying the figures and relative-risk curves were posted on Mendeley Data on 19 September 2018, after publication, and a data-sharing statement was added by correction (Lancet 2018;392:1116).
analysis.selective_reporting: The weighted all-outcome curve on which the headline rests is shown only as an image (Figure 5); the text gives no relative risk, absolute risk or attributable rate at any intake other than its minimum. The single sensitivity analysis of the weights is reported in one sentence without numbers. The search, the study list, the cause-specific curves and model details are in appendices (4.2 MB and 21 MB PDFs) that were not read. The widely reported absolute figures (918 against 914 per 100,000 a year at one drink a day) do not appear in the article; a 2019 letter (Astrup & Estruch) attributes them to The Lancet's press release, which was not found at its cited address.
analysis.power: Not applicable. Uncertainty intervals come from 1000 draws carrying sampling error and modelling uncertainty from hyper-parameter selection and parameter estimation, reported as the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles (Methods › Uncertainty analysis). The paper does not say that they include uncertainty from structural choices (the form of the curves, the weights, the outcomes included) or from residual bias in the underlying observational studies.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Under its inputs and weights, the model attributes about 2.8 million deaths in 2016 to alcohol (2.2% of female and 6.8% of male age-standardised deaths) and ranks alcohol as the leading risk factor at ages 15–49. Of the 23 cause-specific curves, only ischaemic heart disease had a significant J-shape (minimum relative risk 0.86 in men and 0.82 in women at about 0.8–0.9 drinks a day); diabetes and ischaemic stroke dipped non-significantly; all others, including every cancer, rose with intake. The minimum of the single globally DALY-weighted curve was zero drinks a day with an interval reaching 0.8 drinks a day, and it changed significantly only where diabetes and ischaemic heart disease made up more than 60% of deaths.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and the conclusion say the level that minimises health loss is zero and that “the safest level of drinking is none” (Conclusion); the discussion concludes that alcohol leads to health loss in populations whatever the amount drunk (Discussion, 2nd paragraph) and suggests considering recommendations for abstention (Discussion, 4th paragraph). Gaps: (1) the abstract gives the minimum's interval as 0.0–0.8 standard drinks per week, the results as per day, so the abstract understates the uncertainty sevenfold; on the per-day interval, intakes up to 0.8 drinks a day are compatible with the minimum; (2) a curve weighted by global population DALY rates is described as minimising an individual's total attributable risk (Introduction, 7th paragraph; Research in context), although the weights describe the world's disease mix, not a person's, and the authors' own sensitivity analysis shows the curve shifts where ischaemic heart disease and diabetes make up more than 60% of deaths; (3) the interpretation's wording that alcohol 'causes substantial health loss' rests on observational relative risks screened with Bradford Hill's criteria; (4) the discussion treats newer studies showing little or no protection as settling a literature that remains contested. In their 2019 reply to letters, the authors agreed that the risk is low between 0 and 0.8 drinks a day and said that debating zero against near zero misses the point.

timeline.event: Comment by Burton & Sheron in the same issue endorses the conclusions as clear and unambiguous and as support for the UK Chief Medical Officers' guideline (appraised on its own card, sc_burton_2018).

Correction (Lancet 2018;392:1116; DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(18)32338-9), online version corrected 27 September 2018: Alan D Lopez added to the collaborators, two names corrected, one affiliation updated, raw data for the figures and relative-risk curves posted on Mendeley Data (DOI 10.17632/5thy2mcwn7.1) and a data-sharing statement added. No numbers changed.

Letter, Abat, Roussel, Chaudet & Raoult: argue that alcohol consumption tracks life expectancy and SDI, so diseases of ageing were attributed to alcohol; the authors reply that exposure is age-specific and the relative risks control for participants' average age.

Letter, Astrup & Estruch: object that mainly ecological data and models cannot support global policy, that the pooled curve cannot be read at regional or individual level, and that the zero category spans up to 0.8 drinks a day; cite 918 against 914 per 100,000 a year at one drink a day from the press release. Declared ties, as printed: Astrup, external scientific board of and personal fees from the Dutch Beer Institute; Estruch, external scientific board of the Beer and Health Initiative (The Brewers of Europe) and lecture fees from The Brewers of Europe, Fundacion Cerveza y Salud, Pernaud-Ricard and Instituto Cervantes.

Letter, Shield & Rehm: the curves should be weighted by lifetime abstainers' DALYs, not the general population's; with those weights they find a slight net benefit of 20.8 DALYs per 100,000 at one drink (12 g) a day; heavy drinking occasions were not modelled; no competing interests declared. The authors reply that those weights would make the model circular.

Letter, Di Castelnuovo, Costanzo & de Gaetano: all-cause mortality was not analysed; the DALY weighting is unvalidated and somewhat arbitrary (heart failure excluded) and ignores the differing precision of the curves. Declared ties include grants from the European Foundation for Alcohol Research and fees from Heineken and Assobirra. The authors reply that all-cause mortality depends on each population's cause mix.

Authors' reply (Griswold & Gakidou, Lancet 2019;393:2391–92): agree the risk is low between 0 and 0.8 drinks a day, note that most current drinkers drink far more, and call the zero-versus-near-zero debate beside the point.

Second correction (Lancet 2019;393:e44; DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(19)31050-5), online version corrected 20 June 2019: Stefan Lorkowski added to the collaborators with affiliation and declaration of interests. No numbers changed.

GBD 2020 update by the same consortium (Bryazka et al.): with 2020 DALY weights the global, age-standardised TMREL is 0.534 (0–1.00) drinks a day with the 2016 curves and 0.511 (0.400–0.700) with five updated curves; minima between 0 and 0.603 drinks a day at ages 15–39 and J-shaped weighted curves at 40 and older (card sc_bryazka_2022).
Burton & Sheron's comment on GBD 2020 describes the new estimates as seemingly contradicting the 2018 any-amount message (only its first paragraph was readable; the rest is paywalled).

replication.where_it_stands: The 2016 burden figures are model outputs revised by later GBD rounds (the GBD 2020 paper cites 1.78 million alcohol-attributable deaths in 2020 from unpublished GBD 2020 work). The headline zero minimum was not reproduced by the same group's 2022 update, in which the global minimum became about half a standard drink a day once the weights were updated, while minima stayed between 0 and 0.6 drinks a day at ages 15–39. Whether low intake truly lowers the risk of ischaemic heart disease (and of ischaemic stroke and diabetes), the dip that produces every non-zero minimum, is the subject of the cohort and Mendelian-randomization papers on the project list (Wood et al., 2018; Holmes et al., 2014; Millwood et al., 2019; Biddinger et al., 2022; Larsson et al., 2020), appraised by other readers.

funding.funder: Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation (Summary › Funding). The acknowledgments add the US National Institute on Aging (award P30AG047845) and list individual collaborators' fellowships and institutional support, mostly from public research bodies and universities. The funders had no role in design, data collection, analysis, interpretation or writing (Methods › Role of the funding source).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed in the Declaration of interests: Yannick Béjot, grants and personal fees from AstraZeneca and Boehringer-Ingelheim and personal fees from Daiichi-Sankyo, Pfizer, MSD, Medtronic, BMS and Amgen; Jacek Jóźwiak, grants and personal fees from VALEANT, personal fees from ALAB Laboratoria and AMGEN, non-financial support from MICROLIFE and SERVIER; Srinivasa Vittal Katikireddi, grants from the Medical Research Council, the Scottish Government Chief Scientist Office and an NRS Senior Clinical Fellowship during the conduct of the study; Ted Miller, other support from the AB InBev Foundation (ABIF); Maarten Postma, grants, personal fees or other support from 26 pharmaceutical, research and consulting companies; Dan Stein, personal fees or grants from Lundbeck, Novartis, AMBRF, NRGF, Servier, Biocodex, MRC, Cipla and Sun. All except Katikireddi's are stated to be outside the submitted work; all other authors declare no competing interests. The 2019 correction added Stefan Lorkowski, whose declaration appears only in the corrected online version: personal fees from AMGEN, Berlin-Chemie, MSD Sharp & Dohme, Novo Nordisk, Sanofi-Aventis, Synlab, Unilever, Upfield and Akcea Therapeutics and non-financial support from Preventicus, outside the submitted work.
funding.affiliations_note: Analysis led and written at the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (University of Washington); the first author developed the models and ran all analyses (Contributors). The only declared tie bearing an alcohol producer's name is Ted Miller's support from the AB InBev Foundation; one collaborator (Mete Saylan) is an employee of Bayer AG (Acknowledgments). Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: Cause-specific dose–response curves at low intake from designs less exposed to confounding and abstainer bias, chiefly non-linear Mendelian randomization in large cohorts of several ancestries, and cohorts that separate lifetime abstainers from former drinkers and record drinking patterns, combined with a weighting scheme fixed in advance and published with sensitivity analyses of the weights, and checked against all-cause mortality in populations with different disease mixes.

domains.note: Exposure combines sales data (adjusted for tourism and, conservatively, for unrecorded alcohol) with self-reported surveys; burden comes from GBD 2016 cause estimates; harm to others enters only through US road-injury data assumed to apply everywhere; under-15s, drinking patterns, harm to others from violence and outcomes such as dementia are left out, which the authors expect to make the burden an underestimate.

Fitted to observational cohort and case-control estimates (of self-reported intake, as the GBD 2020 paper notes of the same evidence base); reference-group bias adjusted only where a covariate was significant (three outcomes); no quality appraisal of the 592 studies described in the main text; one curve per outcome applied to every population; the low-intake shape for ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke and diabetes is where confounding and abstainer bias are most disputed.

One global curve weighted by 2016 global age-standardised DALY rates, a choice that is not validated and was criticized in 2019 (weights should be abstainers' DALYs; precision of curves ignored); with GBD 2020 DALY weights and the same 2016 curves the global minimum became 0.534 drinks a day (GBD 2020 paper, Table 2).

domains.domain: Uncertainty intervals: what they include and exclude
domains.note: 1000 draws carry sampling error and parameter and hyper-parameter uncertainty; structural choices and residual bias in the underlying studies are not stated to be included; the minimum's interval (0–0.8 drinks a day) is printed per week in the abstract.

One sensitivity analysis (choice of weights) is reported, in a sentence without numbers: the curve changed only where diabetes and ischaemic heart disease exceeded 60% of deaths. No sensitivity to curve form, reference group or outcomes included is reported in the main text; the 2022 update shows the global minimum is sensitive to the weights.

GATHER adherence stated and raw data posted after publication; but the weighted curve appears only as an image, no absolute risks are given, the headline interval has inconsistent units, appendix cross-references conflict, and the methods that matter are only in appendices.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated risk-of-bias instrument exists for burden-of-disease modelling (METHODS §5.3; the round brief sets design 'modelling' with no instrument). The editors' checklist is used with domains for the inputs, the relative-risk curves, the counterfactual level, the uncertainty intervals, the sensitivity of the headline and the reporting, as in card sc_visser_2019; the overall judgment is no milder than the worst domain. The burden estimates are transparent model outputs with stated limitations. The headline zero rests on one globally weighted curve whose interval reaches 0.8 drinks a day and whose minimum moved to about half a drink a day when the same group updated the weights. Citable for GBD 2016's model estimates (attributable deaths and DALYs, drinking prevalence, the cause-specific curve shapes as reported), always with their assumptions; not citable on its own for the statement that any amount of alcohol harms health or that the safest level for a person is zero.

key_findings.finding: Inputs: 121,029 exposure data points from 694 sources; 3,992 relative-risk estimates from 592 prospective and retrospective studies covering about 28 million people and 649,000 registered cases; 23 outcomes; 195 locations, 1990–2016, ages 15 to 95 and older.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data sources, 1st paragraph; Methods › Study design, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: In 2016, 32.5% (95% UI 30.0–35.2) of people worldwide were current drinkers (at least one drink in the past 12 months): 25% (23–27) of females and 39% (36–43) of males, 2.4 billion (2.2–2.6) people. Mean consumption was 0.73 (0.68–0.78) standard drinks (10 g ethanol) a day in females and 1.7 (1.5–1.9) in males.
key_findings.locator: Results › Global, regional, and national trends in alcohol consumption, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The text does not say whether mean consumption is per current drinker or per person; the next paragraph and Figure 2 refer to averages among current drinkers.

key_findings.finding: Current drinking was most common in high-SDI locations (72% [69–75] of females, 83% [80–85] of males) and least common in low-to-middle-SDI locations (8.9% [6.6–9.7] of females, 20% [17–22] of males); examples: Nepal 1.5% (1.2–1.9) of females against 21% (17–25) of males; Sweden 86% (84–88) against 87% (85–89).
key_findings.locator: Results › Global, regional, and national trends in alcohol consumption, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Average consumption among current drinkers (age-standardised): high-SDI locations 1.9 (1.3–2.7) standard drinks a day in females and 2.9 (2.0–4.1) in males; lowest for males in low-SDI locations, 1.4 (0.6–2.4); lowest for females in low-to-middle-SDI locations, 0.3 (0.1–0.6).
key_findings.locator: Results › Global, regional, and national trends in alcohol consumption, 3rd paragraph; Figure 2 legend

key_findings.finding: 2.8 million deaths (95% UI 2.4–3.3) were attributed to alcohol in 2016: 2.2% (1.5–3.0) of age-standardised female deaths and 6.8% (5.8–8.0) of male deaths; 1.6% (1.4–2.0) of female and 6.0% (5.4–6.7) of male DALYs. Alcohol ranked seventh among GBD risk factors.
key_findings.locator: Results › Global patterns in alcohol-attributable deaths and disease burden, 1st paragraph; Summary › Findings

key_findings.finding: At ages 15–49, alcohol was the leading risk factor: 3.8% (3.2–4.3) of female and 12.2% (10.8–13.6) of male deaths, and 2.3% (2.0–2.6) of female and 8.9% (7.8–9.9) of male DALYs, were attributed to it. The leading attributable causes of death in this age group were tuberculosis (1.4% [1.0–1.7] of total deaths), road injuries (1.2% [0.7–1.9]) and self-harm (1.1% [0.6–1.5]).
key_findings.locator: Results › Global patterns in alcohol-attributable deaths and disease burden, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Summary › Findings
key_findings.note: The Results call the 8.9% and 2.3% shares 'of attributable DALYs', the abstract 'attributable DALYs'; the denominator is not stated explicitly (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: At ages 50 and older, cancers made up 27.1% (21.2–33.3) of alcohol-attributable female deaths and 18.9% (15.3–22.6) of alcohol-attributable male deaths in 2016.
key_findings.locator: Results › Global patterns in alcohol-attributable deaths and disease burden, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: In the burden estimates, females, particularly in high-SDI locations, had some net protective effect for ischaemic heart disease and diabetes beyond age 60; among males only high-SDI and low-SDI locations showed a noticeable, small protective effect for ischaemic heart disease.
key_findings.locator: Results › Global patterns in alcohol-attributable deaths and disease burden, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Cause-specific curves (relative to the non-drinking category of the underlying studies): only ischaemic heart disease showed a statistically significant J-shape, with a minimum relative risk of 0.86 (0.80–0.96) in men at 0.83 standard drinks a day and 0.82 (0.72–0.95) in women at 0.92 drinks a day; diabetes and ischaemic stroke showed non-significant J-shapes; no significant age differences were found for ischaemic heart disease or diabetes; every other outcome, including all cancers, rose monotonically with intake.
key_findings.locator: Results › Health risks associated with alcohol consumption, 1st paragraph; Figure 4 (image; values not extracted)

key_findings.finding: The minimum of the DALY-weighted curve over all attributable outcomes (the TMREL) was zero standard drinks a day (95% UI 0.0–0.8 drinks a day), and the weighted risk rose monotonically with intake; the protective associations for ischaemic heart disease and diabetes in females were offset mainly by cancers. In a sensitivity analysis of the weights, the curve changed significantly only where diabetes and ischaemic heart disease made up more than 60% of deaths.
key_findings.locator: Results › Health risks associated with alcohol consumption, 2nd paragraph; Figure 5 (image; values not extracted)
key_findings.note: The abstract prints the same interval as 0.0–0.8 standard drinks per week (reporting issue 1); the GBD 2020 paper (Table 2) and the authors' 2019 reply treat it as per day.

key_findings.finding: Method of the minimum: dose–response curves were fitted with mixed-effects logistic regression and non-linear splines for 0 to 12.5 standard drinks a day; the TMREL is the minimum of a weighted average of the cause-specific curves, weights being each outcome's global age-standardised DALY rate per 100,000 in 2016, both sexes; a covariate for whether former drinkers were in the reference group was retained for ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke and diabetes.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Systematic review and meta-analysis, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Uncertainty intervals are the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of 1000 draws that carry sampling error and modelling uncertainty from hyper-parameter selection and parameter estimation through every step.

Limitations stated by the authors: unrecorded consumption may still be missed; drinking patterns were not modelled; harm to others from road injuries rests on US data; harm to others from violence was not estimated; under-15s were not assessed; outcomes such as dementia and psoriasis were excluded. The authors conclude these make the risks and burden likely underestimates.

Two correction notices changed authorship, an affiliation, a declaration of interests and data availability, not numbers: Lancet 2018;392:1116 (DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(18)32338-9) and Lancet 2019;393:e44 (DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(19)31050-5). The PMC text read is the uncorrected original; every decimal figure in its main text also appears in the corrected online version (editors' comparison of the two texts), so the numbers on this card are the corrected ones.
key_findings.page: PMC HTML; publisher HTML (corrected online version); PMC6902241; PMC6598857
key_findings.locator: Correction notices (Department of Error); corrected version's Data sharing and Declaration of interests

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives the interval of the minimum-risk level as 0.0–0.8 standard drinks per week; the results give the same interval as 0.0–0.8 standard drinks daily. The corrected online version still prints both.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Summary › Findings; Results › Health risks associated with alcohol consumption, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract understates the uncertainty sevenfold (0.8 drinks a day is 5.6 a week). The GBD 2020 paper (Table 2) and the authors' 2019 reply use per day; claims must use the per-day interval.

reporting_issues.issue: The conclusion says alcohol accounts for nearly 10% of global deaths at ages 15–49, but the results give only sex-specific shares (3.8% of female and 12.2% of male deaths); no both-sexes figure is reported.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Conclusion; Results › Global patterns in alcohol-attributable deaths and disease burden, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The 'nearly 10%' figure cannot be checked from the article and should not be cited from it.

reporting_issues.issue: In the Results, the sentence naming tuberculosis, road injuries and self-harm as the leading causes 'in this age group' follows a sentence about the whole lifespan; only the abstract makes clear that the age group is 15–49.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Global patterns in alcohol-attributable deaths and disease burden, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the figures should be cited with the 15–49 age group as stated in Summary › Findings.

reporting_issues.issue: The DALY shares for ages 15–49 are worded as 'of attributable DALYs' in the Results and as 'attributable DALYs were' in the abstract; whether the denominator is all DALYs or DALYs attributable to all risk factors is not stated.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Global patterns in alcohol-attributable deaths and disease burden, 1st paragraph; Summary › Findings
reporting_issues.consequence: Read with the death figures, the shares are most plausibly of all DALYs, but claims should use the deaths figures or state the wording.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion says that in women both ischaemic heart disease and diabetes showed some protection, while the results report a significant J-shape only for ischaemic heart disease and a non-significant one for diabetes.
